name: Hymn to Babylon: 'Literary Texts from the Sippar Library V: A Hymn in Praise of Babylon and the Babylonians' (Anmar A. Fadhil and Enrique Jiménez, Iraq 86)
date: Journal volume dated 2024 (Iraq 86, pp. 21-78); published online by Cambridge University Press on 17 March 2025. LMU press release 'Hymn to Babylon readable again thanks to AI' followed on 28 July 2025, then a second wave of coverage (ScienceDaily, 11 November 2025). The text was read at LMU's Keilschriftwerkstatt in 2023. The main manuscript came from the Sippar Library, excavated by Iraqi archaeologists in 1986. The hymn itself is dated by the editors to the second half of the second millennium BCE (possibly Kassite), with copies from the 7th century to the 2nd/1st century BCE. Sources: https://doi.org/10.1017/irq.2024.23 ; https://www.lmu.de/en/newsroom/news-overview/news/hymn-to-babylon-readable-again-thanks-to-ai-2ae70bee.html ; https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2025/11/251111010011.htm
creator: Anmar A. Fadhil (Assyriologist, head of the Department of Archaeology, College of Arts, University of Baghdad) and Enrique Jiménez (Professor of Ancient Near Eastern Literatures, LMU Munich, head of the electronic Babylonian Library). Transliterations that fed the identification came from the eBL team (Zs. J. Földi, A. Hätinen, T. Mitto, J. Peterson, L. Sáenz, H. Stadhouders, J. Taniguchi) and older handwritten transliterations by A. R. George, W. G. Lambert and W. R. Mayer. Funding: a Gerda Henkel 'Patrimonies' project; tablet conservation under the Bavarian Academy's 'Cuneiform Artefacts from Iraq in Context'. Sources: https://doi.org/10.1017/irq.2024.23 ; https://coart.uobaghdad.edu.iq/?p=30777
form: Open-access critical edition in a peer-reviewed journal (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0): introduction, list of manuscripts, line-by-line score transliteration of every manuscript, normalised Akkadian text, English translation, commentary and photographs. The recovered object is a physical text: a roughly 250-line Akkadian hymn, about two-thirds of which is now recovered. Source: https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/iraq/article/literary-texts-from-the-sippar-library-v-a-hymn-in-praise-of-babylon-and-the-babylonians/B477D54E6554CA35718880339B3736CD
effect_on_arc: This is not a Gilgamesh find, so it changes no character in the epic. What it changes is the picture of Babylonian literature that Gilgamesh sat inside. A 'classic' that literate Babylonians probably knew by heart, copied in schools for some six centuries and quoted in other texts, was entirely unknown until 2025. The editors rank it with Enuma elish, Ludlul and the Hymn to Shamash by number of school excerpts (eleven so far). Its content is surprising: a long description of spring arriving with the Euphrates (one of only two extended nature descriptions in Mesopotamian literature), and praise of Babylonians for protecting orphans, freeing captives and not humiliating the foreigners among them, followed by a passage on three classes of priestesses. For an essay on Gilgamesh the point is that the canon is still moving: if a text this popular could vanish so thoroughly, the gaps in Gilgamesh are not the only holes in the record. Source: https://doi.org/10.1017/irq.2024.23
critical_response: Peer review was conventional and thorough: the editors thank M. Frazer and an anonymous reviewer, and the edition collated tablets in Berlin and London. Press coverage was large and uniformly positive: phys.org, ScienceAlert, Archaeology Magazine, Artnet, ZME Science, La Brújula Verde, The Wild Hunt and ScienceDaily. Most headlines credit AI ('AI revives lost 3,000-year-old Babylonian hymn'). Jiménez's own framing: 'With our AI-supported platform, we were able to identify thirty additional manuscripts that belong to the rediscovered hymn, a process that would have taken decades in the past.' On the nature passage he said: 'That is spectacular, because only a few descriptions of nature from Mesopotamia have survived.' I found no scholarly critique of the edition [uncertain]. Sources: https://phys.org/news/2025-07-hymn-babylon-millennium.html ; https://archaeologymag.com/2025/07/hymn-to-babylon-discovered/ ; https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2025/11/251111010011.htm ; https://news.artnet.com/art-world/babylonian-hymn-resurfaces-ai-2664269
controversies: No dispute over the text or its provenance. The friction is in the numbers and in the word 'AI'. The paper's abstract says 20 manuscripts; its acknowledgements say the eBL made it possible 'to use 21 manuscripts, consisting of 31 fragments'; the press release turned this into 'thirty additional manuscripts', which conflates fragments with manuscripts. Headlines also disagree on age: 'missing for a millennium', 'last read 2,000 years ago', '3,000-year-old'. None of the popular pieces explains that the 'AI' is the eBL Fragmentarium's string-alignment search over human transliterations, not a model reading clay; the journal article itself never uses the words artificial intelligence and credits the eBL platform and the people who transliterated the fragments. The paper also records that the Sippar Library room was probably robbed and walled up in antiquity, which is why the two halves of the main tablet were found in different niches. The reading of the press conflation is mine, not a published critique [uncertain]. Sources: https://doi.org/10.1017/irq.2024.23 ; https://phys.org/news/2025-07-hymn-babylon-millennium.html ; https://www.lmu.de/en/newsroom/news-overview/news/hymn-to-babylon-readable-again-thanks-to-ai-2ae70bee.html
regional_reception: Strong Iraqi ownership. The co-author is Iraqi, the key tablet is in the Iraq Museum and published with permission of the University of Baghdad's College of Arts and the State Board of Antiquities and Heritage, and the University of Baghdad published an Arabic piece titled 'Babylon is reborn (a rediscovered hymn and the city's legacy)'. Arabic social media (e.g. the Mutanabbi Street Facebook page) celebrated Fadhil's achievement. LMU reports colleagues from Babylon telling Jiménez 'You make us proud to be Babylonians.' The work sits inside an ongoing LMU-Baghdad programme to decipher hundreds of Sippar Library tablets. Sources: https://coart.uobaghdad.edu.iq/?p=30777 ; https://www.lmu.de/en/newsroom/news-overview/news/hymn-to-babylon-readable-again-thanks-to-ai-2ae70bee.html
method: Conventional cuneiform scholarship accelerated by fragment search. Fadhil and Jiménez started from the Sippar Library tablet IM.132512 + IM.132667 (joined earlier by Hilgert), conserved and photographed in Baghdad. Its text was searched against the eBL Fragmentarium, where team members had already transliterated thousands of British Museum fragments from photographs. The Fragmentarium's alignment search (built to tolerate cuneiform's variant spellings) matched duplicates scattered across collections: Neo-Babylonian library tablets from Sippar and Babylon, three Late Babylonian tablets from Babylon, one Assyrian school tablet in Berlin (VAT.10174, known since 1925 but never recognised as this text), and ten Babylonian school excerpts. Humans then confirmed matches, made joins (BabLB1 alone combines nine BM fragments), collated originals, built a line-by-line score, and translated. Sources: https://doi.org/10.1017/irq.2024.23 ; https://theconversation.com/ai-is-helping-us-read-ancient-mesopotamian-literature-205091
ai_pipeline_stage: Fragment matching only: the eBL search proposed which transliterated fragments duplicate the hymn. Imaging was by museum photographers, transliteration by named Assyriologists (some from handwritten notes by George, Lambert and Mayer), and joining, collation, reconstruction and translation were human. Sources: https://doi.org/10.1017/irq.2024.23
scale_metrics: About 250 lines originally; roughly two-thirds recovered completely or partially (lines 1 to about 159 well preserved; about 100 lines of the end missing or damaged). 20 manuscripts in the abstract, 21 manuscripts from 31 fragments in the acknowledgements: 4 Neo-Babylonian from Sippar, 3 Neo-Babylonian from Babylon, 3 Late Babylonian from Babylon, 1 Assyrian school tablet, 3 Sippar and 7 Babylon school tablets. A further 16 BM fragments may belong to unrecovered sections. Manuscripts run from the 7th century BCE (Assur school tablet) to the 2nd/1st century BCE. Main Sippar tablet: 20.5 x 12.6 x 2.1 cm, four columns, with decimal markers every ten lines. Eleven school excerpts, compared with 74 for Enuma elish and 16 for Ludlul. Press: 'a process that would have taken decades'. Sources: https://doi.org/10.1017/irq.2024.23 ; https://archaeologymag.com/2025/07/hymn-to-babylon-discovered/
what_was_found: A previously unknown Akkadian 'great hymn' in praise of Marduk, his temple Esagil, the city of Babylon and the Babylonians. Sections: opening hymn to Marduk (1-25); a god's speech praising Marduk, ending with Anu, Enlil and Ea blessing him (26-85); hymn to Esagil (86-99); hymn to Babylon as a hoard of gems, with its wall Imgur-Enlil, its primeval king Alulu, and the Euphrates bringing spring (100-124); hymn to the Babylonians and their priestesses, ending 'These are the ones freed by Marduk' (125-159); a broken final section. It may be linked by catchline to the Hymn to Shamash, forming a series. It is outside Gilgamesh; its place in this project is as the cleanest demonstration of the eBL method that is also recovering Gilgamesh. Source: https://doi.org/10.1017/irq.2024.23
provenance_and_ethics: Fully legitimate. The key tablet was excavated by an Iraqi team at Sippar (Abu Habbah) in 1986, stays in the Iraq Museum in Baghdad, and was conserved in Iraq under a Bavarian Academy project. The other manuscripts are registered 19th-century museum holdings: British Museum consignments from Sippar and Babylon (1880s), one tablet in Istanbul (Scheil's Sippar excavations) and one in Berlin's Vorderasiatisches Museum (from Assur). The split mirrors colonial collecting: most duplicates sit in London, the best copy in Baghdad, and the join happens digitally in Munich. The edition is open access and eBL photographs and transliterations are online. Sources: https://doi.org/10.1017/irq.2024.23 ; https://www.lmu.de/en/newsroom/news-overview/news/hymn-to-babylon-readable-again-thanks-to-ai-2ae70bee.html
ai_craft_tension: This is the clearest case of where the machine helps and where it stops. The search engine found duplicates no one had connected, including a Berlin school tablet edited in 1925 and read for decades as part of the Erra Epic or an anonymous 'praise song to Babylon'. That step used to take a lifetime of memory; now it takes a query. Yet the search only worked because people had first typed 31 fragments into the database, some from Lambert's and George's handwritten notes, and because a conservator in Baghdad cleaned the main tablet. After the matches came the real reading: noticing that fire, air and water map onto Anu, Enlil and Ea; tying the first king Alulu to Berossus; dating the poem from its kind words about Elamite priests. The press said 'AI revives hymn'. The paper thanks the eBL platform and names the people. For Lee's essay, the line is that the machine found the pages, and two scholars, one in Baghdad and one in Munich, worked out what the poem says.
essay_hooks: (1) A school classic that vanished: 'The hymn was copied by children at school. It's unusual that such a popular text in its day was unknown to us before now' (Jiménez, phys.org, July 2025). (2) Hidden in plain sight: a Berlin school tablet published in 1925 turned out to be part of this hymn. (3) Babylonians who 'do not humiliate' the foreigners among them, and who free the captive 'even at the cost of a silver talent' (lines 135, 139, Fadhil and Jiménez translation). (4) The Euphrates 'quenches the lea, saturates the canebrake' (line 117): one of only two long descriptions of spring in Mesopotamian literature. (5) Late Babylonians in a half-empty city still copying a poem about Babylon as 'a gem-laden mountain' (editors' phrase). (6) 'Without the eBL platform... it would be impossible for this edition to use 21 manuscripts, consisting of 31 fragments' (acknowledgements), versus the press's 'thirty additional manuscripts'. (7) 'You make us proud to be Babylonians' (Iraqi colleagues to Jiménez, LMU). (8) The main tablet's two halves were found in different niches of a library robbed in antiquity. Sources: https://doi.org/10.1017/irq.2024.23 ; https://phys.org/news/2025-07-hymn-babylon-millennium.html ; https://archaeologymag.com/2025/07/hymn-to-babylon-discovered/ ; https://www.lmu.de/en/newsroom/news-overview/news/hymn-to-babylon-readable-again-thanks-to-ai-2ae70bee.html
